title: Flow-aware KV remap for tensor/pipeline boundaries
creator: Evelyn Chan
description:
Problem: In mixed tensor/pipeline parallel topologies we observe KV cache memory fragmentation and hot-slice concentration that causes per-GPU OOMs and uneven latency under continuous batching. Pipeline boundaries create affinities where consecutive requests touch overlapping KV regions on different GPUs, causing cross-GPU synchronization and stalls. Existing slab/stripe schemes either (a) enforce rigid interleaving that increases cross-device copies, or (b) compact per-GPU slabs that cannot adapt to shifting request flows and heterogeneous GPU memory sizes.

Proposal: Implement a flow-aware KV remapping layer that dynamically relocates and remaps KV slices to GPUs based on observed request flow affinity and tensor/pipeline boundaries. Key ideas:
- Flow hashing: maintain lightweight flow IDs per client-session or prompt prefix and track hot KV keys by flow.
- Affinity-aware placement: prefer placing hot KV slices on GPUs that are on the same pipeline stage or tensor-parallel peers most frequently accessed by that flow.
- Epoched directory: maintain a compact directory (per-model) with versioned slice-to-GPU mappings; remaps are published via small epoch increments to avoid global locks.
- Incremental remap: move hot slices asynchronously with double-buffered pointers in the directory and coordinated small metadata barrier, avoiding full KV copy pause.
- Prefetch hints: integrate with continuous batching controller to issue prefetches to target GPUs when a flow is predicted to access moved slices within the next N micro-batches.
- Heterogeneous-aware sizing: compute target slab sizes per GPU proportional to free memory and predicted flow weight; support spill-to-CPU as controlled fallback.
- Latency SLO guardrails: remap actions bounded by budgeted time-per-remap and throttled when p99 latency approaches threshold.

Design tradeoffs and rationale:
- Pros: reduces cross-GPU synchronization and remote KV lookups for stable flows, improves memory utilization on heterogeneous clusters, and reduces tail latency under continuous batching.
- Cons: increased metadata complexity and potential for transient extra memory usage during slice migration. Prefetching risks wasted bandwidth if flow predictions are wrong.

Integration points:
- Batching controller: expose prefetch API and flow signal hooks.
- KV allocator: add per-GPU target slab calculator and asynchronous mover.
- Directory service: lightweight distributed epoch publish/subscribe (reuse existing model-metadata channel).
- Rollout strategy: start with canary model and disabled prefetch, enable remap only when memory pressure or hot-slice skew detected.

Metrics to monitor:
- p50/p95/p99 latency per model and per-flow
- cross-GPU KV lookup rate
- remap churn (slices remapped per minute)
- memory headroom per GPU
- bandwidth used for remap and prefetch

Deliverables:
- design doc with interface for flow signals and directory protocol (Confluence)
- implementation: directory + mover + allocator hooks + batching controller integration
- canary rollout plan and dashboards
- benchmark report comparing baseline slab-striping vs flow-remap under heterogeneous nodes
acceptance_criteria:
1) New directory API implemented and documented; remap epoch changes observable in model metadata channel.
2) Asynchronous mover moves hot slices without blocking inference (no >50ms stall observed during migration in canary).
3) Integration with continuous-batching controller to issue prefetch hints; end-to-end prefetch results in >=20% reduction in remote KV lookups for targeted flows in canary.
4) Demo canary on two heterogeneous clusters showing reduced p99 by at least 15% for long-tail flows and no increase in overall GPU OOM rate.
5) Dashboard panels created for remap churn, cross-GPU lookups, and remap bandwidth.
6) Rollout runbook and automatic throttle when p99 > configured SLO.
